questions.q: What is the truth value of the compound statement "2 + 2 = 4 and 3 × 3 = 10"? Identify the component statements and explain your reasoning.
questions.a: The compound statement is FALSE. Component statements: p: "2 + 2 = 4" (TRUE), q: "3 × 3 = 10" (FALSE). Since p ∧ q requires both p and q to be true, and q is false, the conjunction is false. A wrong answer (e.g., saying it's true because the first part is true) reveals the student thinks "and" only needs one true component, confusing it with "or".

questions.q: Consider the statement: "x > 5 or x < 3". For which real values of x is this statement true? Explain why the inclusive "or" matters here.
questions.a: The statement is true for x ∈ (-∞, 3) ∪ (5, ∞). At x = 3 or x = 5, one component is false and the other is false, so the disjunction is false. There is NO x that makes both components true simultaneously (no x is both >5 and <3), so inclusive vs exclusive or gives the same result here. A wrong answer (e.g., saying "all real numbers" or "x ≠ 3,5") reveals the student doesn't understand how to combine solution sets with "or" (union) or thinks "or" means exactly one is true (exclusive or).

questions.q: Let p: "Triangle ABC is equilateral", q: "Triangle ABC is isosceles". Write the compound statement p ∧ q in words and determine its truth value for: (i) an equilateral triangle, (ii) an isosceles but not equilateral triangle, (iii) a scalene triangle.
questions.a:
p ∧ q: "Triangle ABC is equilateral AND triangle ABC is isosceles."
(i) Equilateral triangle: p=T, q=T (every equilateral is isosceles) → p ∧ q = TRUE
(ii) Isosceles but not equilateral: p=F, q=T → p ∧ q = FALSE
(iii) Scalene triangle: p=F, q=F → p ∧ q = FALSE
A wrong answer for (i) (saying FALSE because "equilateral and isosceles are different") reveals the student doesn't know the mathematical hierarchy (equilateral ⊂ isosceles) and treats them as mutually exclusive categories.

questions.q: Compare the truth tables of p ∧ q and p ∨ q. For which rows do they give the same truth value? What does this tell you about the relationship between "and" and "or"?
questions.a: Truth table rows (p, q): (T,T)→both T; (T,F)→∧=F, ∨=T; (F,T)→∧=F, ∨=T; (F,F)→both F. They match only when p and q have the SAME truth value (both T or both F). This reveals that p ∧ q and p ∨ q are equivalent exactly when p and q are logically equivalent (p ↔ q). A wrong answer (e.g., "they never match" or "they match when one is true") shows the student hasn't actually constructed both tables side-by-side or doesn't understand "same truth value" means identical output for identical input.

questions.q: A student writes: "The negation of 'p and q' is 'not p and not q'." Is this correct? If not, give the correct negation and explain the error using a concrete example.
questions.a: Incorrect. The correct negation of p ∧ q is ¬p ∨ ¬q (De Morgan's Law). Example: p="It is raining", q="It is cold". "It is raining and it is cold" negated is "It is NOT raining OR it is NOT cold" (at least one fails). The student's version "not raining AND not cold" is stronger - it requires BOTH to fail, which is not the logical negation. This error reveals the student distributes negation incorrectly (like ¬(p∧q) = ¬p∧¬q) instead of flipping the connective, a classic algebraic misconception.

questions.q: Create a real-life situation (Indian context) where the inclusive "or" and exclusive "or" give DIFFERENT practical outcomes. Write both compound statements symbolically and explain the difference.
questions.a: Good answer: "You can pay by UPI or card" at a shop. Inclusive: p ∨ q (accepts UPI, card, or both split payment). Exclusive: (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q) (must choose exactly one). Difference: split payment allowed in inclusive, forbidden in exclusive. Poor answer: vague scenario without clear p, q definition or confusion between logical and practical exclusivity. Reveals student can't distinguish mathematical "or" (inclusive by default) from everyday "or" (often exclusive).
